Chapter 4: The Wounds of the Father and the Need for Male Mentorship
Think back for a moment to when you were a kid. Did you ever look up to your dad, hoping for some kind of sign—approval, a nod, maybe just a sense of what being a man was supposed to look like? For a lot of us, that connection with our fathers just wasn’t there. Sometimes dads were physically gone, or maybe they were right there in the room but felt miles away. And sometimes, they had their own struggles that just got in the way.
What happens when that connection is missing? Well, it leaves a kind of wound. Not always something you see on the surface, but it’s there—a gap, a sense that something’s missing even if you can’t quite put your finger on what.
This wound can show up in all sorts of ways. Maybe it’s anger, or always feeling like you just don’t measure up. For others, it’s more like a quiet sadness, or a longing for real connection that never seems to come. A lot of guys end up searching for mentors—older men who can give the kind of support and guidance that was missing at home.
In the story of Iron John, there’s this young prince whose relationship with his father isn’t easy. The king is distant—he cares more about keeping things in order than really seeing his son for who he is. But then there’s the wild man, who’s a totally different kind of mentor. He leads with experience, with challenge, and with a willingness to step into the unknown.
The truth is, not having real mentorship is one of the biggest challenges for men today. Without it, it’s easy to just drift—never really sure how to make that leap from being a boy to becoming a man. The old rituals that used to mark this transition have faded away, replaced by a lot of trial and error. Some guys find their way through sports, or the military, or some other structured path. Others turn to books, therapy, or spiritual practices. But that longing—for someone who gets it, who can say, “Hey, I’ve been through this. I understand”—that’s still there.
Let me tell you about one man. He grew up with a father who was always at work. He became the classic overachiever—did great in school, tried to make everyone happy—but deep down, he felt invisible. Things started to change when he met an older colleague who took the time to listen, share stories, and offer honest feedback. It wasn’t some official mentorship program—just a real relationship built on trust and respect.
Then there’s another story—a man whose father was always there physically, but never really opened up emotionally. He learned early on to keep his feelings hidden, to be “strong” and “independent.” But the cost? His relationships suffered, and he often felt alone. Things only started to shift when he joined a men’s group, where he could finally talk about his struggles and hear from others going through the same thing.
Here’s something to pay attention to: this wound of the father isn’t just one person’s problem. It’s a cultural thing. As society has changed, a lot of men have lost touch with the sources of guidance and support that helped previous generations grow. The result? A kind of collective confusion—a sense that something important has slipped away.
The story of Iron John tells us that healing this wound takes more than just working on yourself. It’s about finding real community, and building relationships that are honest, open, and supportive. The wild man shows us what that looks like—he doesn’t hand out easy answers. Instead, he challenges you, supports you, and encourages you to grow.
So, what happens when you seek out mentors—whether through friendships, work, or community? The journey to manhood becomes a little less lonely, and a lot more meaningful. The wounds from the past are still there, but now they’re part of a bigger story—a story about growth, healing, and real connection.
In a world where independence is often valued above all else, the need for mentorship has never been more important. The story of Iron John reminds us: none of us is meant to make this journey alone. The wild man—waiting just at the edge of the forest—is both a guide and a companion. He’s a reminder that the path to maturity is one we’re meant to walk together.
